transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

Well, I guess what finally pushed me to come in is these little routines I keep getting stuck in. Like, I’ll handle my wrist brace and then feel like I need to wash my hands again, even if I just did. And before I leave the house I’ll recheck the stove, the front door… sometimes I’m silently counting through steps in my head.

It sounds silly when I say it out loud—I used to be very organized, you know, graduate school sort of trained that into me, though my wife used to say I could turn making coffee into a procedure—but lately it’s not just being careful. It’s making me late, even when part of me knows I’ve already done enough.
Do these routines or the need to repeat actions cause you anxiety or distress, especially if you feel you can’t complete them?

Yes, it does. Not every single time, but if I’m trying to leave and I haven’t done the little sequence—wash after touching the wrist brace, check the stove, check the front door, count through things in my head—I get this keyed-up feeling, like I can’t quite move on.

And the odd thing is, I know I already checked. I’ll even remember checking. But then I think, well, did I really look closely enough? My wife used to tease me about being methodical—graduate school habits, I suppose—but this is different. It’s not useful organizing anymore. It makes me late, and that’s when I get upset with myself.

Have you been experiencing any persistent, unwanted thoughts or images that come to mind and feel difficult to control, which might be connected to these routines or actions you feel you need to repeat?

Yes… yes, I think that’s part of it. I’ll be sitting at home reading, or getting myself ready to go in for a museum shift—funny, I used to be able to lose an hour just reading exhibit notes—and then this ugly little thought barges in. Like I’ve left something unsafe, or I touched something unclean, or somehow I’ve put someone at risk.

And I do know, rationally, that it’s out of proportion. I know that. But the thought doesn’t really ask permission, it just sort of lands there and then I feel like I have to do something about it.
Do these intrusive thoughts or the routines you feel you need to do take up more than an hour of your day?

I’m not sure I’ve ever timed it properly. It feels longer when I’m in the middle of it, if that makes sense. Like when you’re waiting for a kettle to boil and suddenly you notice every little sound in the kitchen—my wife used to say I could make tea into an event.

But, an hour… I don’t know. Some days maybe it’s just bits and pieces scattered around, and other days it feels like it eats into the morning. I’d have to actually keep track to answer you honestly.
Have these thoughts and routines been affecting your ability to function in your daily life, such as at work or in your relationships?

Yes, somewhat. I mean, I’m still managing by myself day to day—meals, errands, keeping the house in reasonable order, all that. Though “reasonable” is a flexible word, my wife used to have a much sharper eye for where things belonged.

But it has affected things. I’ve been late to my docent shifts at the museum because getting out the door turns into… well, into a whole production. And I’ve skipped a few museum events too, not because I didn’t want to go, exactly, but because by the time I started trying to leave, it just felt like too much to get through all of it.
Have these thoughts and routines been causing you significant emotional distress, even outside of the impact on your daily routine or activities?

Yes, it does upset me. What brings me in, really, is that I’ve gotten stuck doing these little routines—washing my hands again after handling my wrist brace, rechecking the stove and the front door, counting through the steps in my head before I leave.

And it’s silly, because I know I’ve already done enough. I’ll stand there thinking, “You checked it, you know you checked it,” but I still feel wound up until I do it again. Then I’m late, and I get irritated with myself… and then of course that doesn’t help anything. My wife used to say I could turn a five-minute departure into a small military campaign. These days it’s less funny when it’s just me standing by the door doing it.
Can you tell me if these intrusive thoughts or routines are something you feel you have to do to prevent something bad from happening, or to reduce your anxiety, even if it’s just temporary relief?

Yes… I think that’s right. It’s not that I truly believe the house will burn down every time, exactly, but when I recheck the stove or the front door, it’s like I’m trying to settle that feeling that something’s been left wrong.

And the handwashing after I handle my wrist brace—well, I’ll tell myself it’s probably fine, but then I feel uneasy until I wash again. Same with counting through the steps before I leave. I know I’ve already done enough, but doing it again gives me a little relief… only for a while. Then it can start over, and suddenly I’m late. Funny, I used to be early for everything. My wife always liked to arrive before the doors opened, especially at museum lectures. Now just getting out the front door can feel like its own lecture series.
Are there times when your intrusive thoughts or the things you feel you need to do aren’t specifically about safety, cleanliness, or preventing harm, but something else entirely?

I’m not sure, honestly. I can’t think of a clear example that’s outside those sorts of things—safety, cleanliness, that kind of worry.

I mean, I do get particular about things sometimes, but I’ve always been a bit particular. My wife used to tease me about how I’d line up the museum brochures on the kitchen table after bringing them home, but that felt more like habit than… whatever this is. So no, I don’t think there’s some separate kind of thought I’m doing it for. Not that I’ve noticed, anyway.
Do you ever feel the need to arrange things in a certain way, or repeat actions until they feel exactly right, even if it’s not about safety or cleanliness?

Well… not so much arranging things just so, I don’t think. I mean, I’ve always liked things neat enough—my wife used to say I’d straighten a stack of mail before I’d read it—but that’s not really what’s bringing me in.

It’s more these little routines I get stuck in. Washing my hands again after I’ve handled my wrist brace, checking the stove and the front door, counting through the steps in my head before I leave. I know I’ve done it already, that’s the frustrating part, but I still end up repeating it until I feel like I can move on. And then I’m late, which never used to be like me.

Do you ever feel the need to repeat actions or have intrusive thoughts related to things not feeling quite right unless they are done a certain way, like needing to do something until it feels balanced or exact?

I suppose… not really in the “balanced” or “exact” way, like lining things up until they feel symmetrical. It’s more that I get stuck repeating the same little routines.

Like I’ll wash my hands again after handling my wrist brace, or go back and check the stove and the front door, or count through the steps in my head before I leave. And I know I’ve already done enough—that’s the irritating part—but I still feel like I can’t quite move on until I do it again. Then before I know it I’m late, which is frustrating because I used to be very punctual. My wife and I were always the sort of people who got places early, you know, found good seats and all that.
